# Core Values Behavioral Round

[← Airbnb](../README.md) · [Every Airbnb question](../../airbnb.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/core-values-bq-round)

`bq` `culture-fit` `star` `values` `why-company`

---

## Requirements

- It is scheduled independently of the technical loop and commonly follows a favorable onsite result.
- The format is a discussion rather than a STAR-style exercise, and the interviewer evaluates against the company’s culture framework.
- Common question areas include:
  - Why Airbnb in particular? (Its mission, connection to the product, or a personal travel story.)
  - What is the world’s largest problem, and what are you doing about it?
  - Airbnb travel experiences that made a lasting impression.
  - How you choose accommodation and how you respond when an experience goes badly.
  - Examples of collaborating across cultures or time zones.
  - Senior engineers or mentors who influenced your development.
  - Times you took a risk in your personal life or career.
  - Moving from coding to project ownership — what made that change most difficult?
  - Obstacles or uncertainties you expect from working at Airbnb.
  - What it means to be both a host and a guest, supported by a specific personal story.
  - Something you failed to deliver, your greatest challenge, and an inventive idea for changing the world.
  - An occasion when you received difficult feedback and one when you delivered it.
- Hobbies and side projects may also be discussed; some candidates say the entire set of questions took 20 minutes and that the interview finished ahead of time — an early finish is not a negative indication.

## Notes

- The round rewards genuineness and self-knowledge rather than memorized corporate language. Broad replies such as “I want to make an impact” tend to be weaker than precise ones such as “the Cuba pop-up listing in 2018 changed how my family travels.”
- Senior candidates say they have been asked to describe a values-based choice from an earlier job where following the immediate local incentive would have led to another decision.
- The mission-focused group of questions (“the world’s biggest problem” and “what is your cause?”) serves as a calibration check; the interviewer does not expect one particular response, but does look for evidence that you have considered the issue.
- Unusual and original prompts appear, and candidates have described this round as refreshing compared with the AI-pattern behavioral interviews used elsewhere.
- The hiring committee treats the values interview as a deciding factor, with strong technical performance paired with weak values alignment being a frequent rejection route.
- Recruiters directly advise candidates beforehand not to invent stories — one repeated warning involves a candidate who said they loved travel but could not identify anywhere they had visited. Since authenticity is tested, base every response on something you have genuinely done.

## Preparation

- Draft three personal-story threads tied to Airbnb’s mission: a meaningful travel experience, a project in which you chose according to your values, and someone who influenced your working style.
- Read the latest founder or shareholder letter from Airbnb — language that matches the company’s current narrative can signal preparation.
- Rehearse your “why Airbnb” response until it fits within 90 seconds, removing anything that feels broad or interchangeable.
- Prepare a single-paragraph response to “what is the world’s biggest problem?” — choose an issue you truly care about rather than one that merely sounds admirable.
- Rehearse with someone outside the industry; if they find your story unnatural, revise it.
